node.label: Joy Parr
node.date_label: Labouring Children 1980 · 'Nature and Hierarchy' 1985 · The Gender of Breadwinners 1990 · 'Gender History and Historical Practice' 1995 · Domestic Goods 1999 · Sensing Changes 2010
node.description: A Canadian historian of work, gender, childhood, consumption and the environment. In 1985 she wrote that what set women and children apart as historical subjects was not nature but 'proximity to power', and asked historians to 'allow as a possibility that gender/sex hierarchies and class hierarchies function simultaneously, each according to its own logic, often in conflict'. The Gender of Breadwinners (1990) tested this in two Ontario towns, Paris, a knitting-mill town where most wage earners were women, and Hanover, a furniture town where most were men; reviewers quote it rejecting 'an ahistorical hierarchy of oppressions' and treating 'class/gender, male/female, market/nonmarket, public/private' as pairs whose meanings 'are multiple and mutable'. In the Left History exchange of 1995–96 Iacovetta and Kealey called her 'a major figure in the field' of gender history, while Sangster criticised the tie her 1995 essay drew between gender history and 'the post-structuralist premise that identities were made in relationships'; the labour historian Craig Heron praised the book but found that it had 'suppressed the impact of class' in a 1949 strike. Labouring Children (1980) grew from her Yale thesis on British child immigrants; later books turned to postwar household goods (Domestic Goods, 1999) and to sensory histories of megaprojects and environmental change (Sensing Changes, 2010).
node.representative_figures_and_works: Joy Parr (1949–2024); PhD Yale 1977 ('The Home Children: British Juvenile Immigrants to Canada, 1868–1924'); Labouring Children: British Immigrant Apprentices to Canada, 1869–1924 (1980); Childhood and Family in Canadian History (ed., 1982); “Nature and Hierarchy: Reflections on Writing the History of Women and Children” (Atlantis, 1985); “Disaggregating the Sexual Division of Labour” (CSSH, 1988); The Gender of Breadwinners: Women, Men, and Change in Two Industrial Towns, 1880–1950 (1990); “Gender History and Historical Practice” (CHR, 1995; reprinted in Gender and History in Canada, ed. with Mark Rosenfeld, 1996); “Household Choices as Politics and Pleasure in 1950s Canada” (ILWCH, 1999); Domestic Goods: The Material, the Moral, and the Economic in the Postwar Years (1999). After 2000: “Smells Like?” (Environmental History, 2006); Sensing Changes: Technologies, Environments, and the Everyday, 1953–2003 (2010). Readings: Drystek (1980); Heron, Guildford, Scheinberg and Dennis (1991); Bertaux (1992); Benson (1993); the Left History exchange (Sangster 1995, 1996; Dubinsky and Marks 1996; Iacovetta and Kealey 1996); Brush (2000); Owram (2001); Jackson and Rumiel (2011).
node.scope_note: Her own words are read in 'Nature and Hierarchy' (Atlantis, 1985, pp. 39–44, in full), the first-page extract of the 1988 CSSH article and the abstract of the 1999 ILWCH article. Her books are not read here: The Gender of Breadwinners, Domestic Goods and Sensing Changes are quoted only as their reviewers quote them, with the reviewers' page references, and the 1995 CHR essay only as Iacovetta and Kealey (1996) and Sangster (1996) quote it. In-period reviews read in full: Drystek (1980), Heron (CHR, 1991), Guildford (Atlantis, 1991), Scheinberg (Archivaria, 1991), Dennis (EcHR, 1991), Bertaux (JEH, 1992), Benson (JAH, 1993), Brush (EH.NET, 2000); later reception: Owram (BC Studies, 2001); the four Left History papers of 1995–96 are read in full. She is not presented as a founder: her 1985 essay places itself among 'a good many others' asking for the change, and the Canadian gender-history debate also turned on Pierson (1991) and Scott. The 1995 CHR essay appeared in an issue of historiographical essays, not in a CHR exchange; the exchange that took it up was in Left History. The environmental work dates from 2006–10 and is used only for the environment edge; a 2026 CHR forum on The Gender of Breadwinners is a later reading.

proposed_edges.relationship: Gender and class as simultaneous hierarchies, and gender history as a practice in Canadian women's history (1985–96)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: In-period, her own words (Atlantis, 1985, read in full): women and children are not tied together as subjects by nature; 'What distinguishes feminine and preschooler from masculine and prime of life is not naturalness versus artificiality but proximity to power' (p. 39). She criticises the mid-1970s Canadian literature on reform for characterising 1880–1920 as 'an era of "maternal feminism"', seeing women's public actions 'definitionally as an extension of the private' (p. 41), and asks historians to 'stop shying away from the word "patriarchy"' and to 'allow as a possibility that gender/sex hierarchies and class hierarchies function simultaneously, each according to its own logic, often in conflict' (p. 44). She presents this as a change 'a good many others have already begun to suggest' (p. 39). The Gender of Breadwinners (1990), unread here, as reviewers quote it: Guildford (Atlantis, 1991, p. 140) says she rejects 'an ahistorical hierarchy of oppressions' (p. 8) and argues 'that class and gender are made and experienced simultaneously'; Bertaux (JEH, 1992, p. 241) quotes p. 9 on 'these galloping pairs—class/gender, male/female, market/nonmarket, public/private' whose meanings 'are multiple and mutable'. Reception in the Left History exchange (all read in full): Sangster calls the book 'One of the path breaking books on gender history' (1995, p. 120); Iacovetta and Kealey call her 'recognized as a leading practitioner of gender history' (1996, p. 222) and 'a major figure in the field', quoting her 1995 CHR essay (pp. 362–63) that 'gender history made masculinity and femininity commensurably problematical historically, while insisting that neither could be well understood without companion inquiries into the other hierarchies with which they were mutually intertwined' (p. 228); Dubinsky and Marks cite her for refraining 'from imposing one category - be it class or gender - on historical actors' (1996, p. 211). Criticism: Sangster (1996, p. 240 n. 2) characterises Parr's essay (its reprint in Gender and History in Canada, 1996, p. 11, unread here) as placing critics 'feminist and anti-feminist alike, in the same oppositional group' (Sangster's wording, not a quotation from Parr), notes that she had been reproached for not offering 'more criticism of historians such as Mariana Valverde and Joy Parr' (p. 240 n. 3), and, quoting Parr's line that the move to gender 'began from the post-structuralist premise that identities were made in relationships' (reprint p. 14), questions 'the prevailing assumption that gender history as the field, post-structuralism as the method, equals a superior, more broad-minded history' (pp. 244, 246). The 1995 essay itself is unread: its words here are quoted by Iacovetta and Kealey and by Sangster. Not a founding: the field's gender debate also runs through Pierson (1991) and Scott (edge_891). Later reading, labelled: a 2026 CHR 'great books' forum (abstract only) calls the book 'a path-breaking study that challenged established dichotomies in social theory'.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: gender_category_debate holds Parr with the 1995 essay and the Left History papers, now read for this entry. Its focus says 'The replies were not read; their positions are not characterised further'; that sentence could be revised at release (this draft does not edit it). work_family_state (the 1990 book) is the alternative; postwar_domesticity is served by edge 5.

proposed_edges.relationship: Gender in the making of class: a women's town and a men's town, Paris and Hanover, Ontario (1985–90)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: In-period, her own words (Atlantis, 1985): 'students of men's work and men's participation in labour organisations', with women's historians and historians of childhood, 'have reified the skill-unskill boundary' (p. 42); 'Skill, too, is a socially constructed category' (pp. 42–43). Of the Marxist analysis in Women at Work, Ontario, 1850–1930 (1975) she writes, quoting feminist critics (n. 20: Phillips and Taylor; Hartmann), that it 'explains why a hierarchy of labour is necessary within the waged labour force, but tells us nothing about why women end up at the bottom of this hierarchy' (p. 43). The Gender of Breadwinners (1990; unread here) compares Paris and Hanover, Ontario. Heron, a labour historian, reviewing it (CHR, 1991, read in full): 'the most exhilarating, challenging book to appear in modern Canadian social history in many years'; it 'integrates and surpasses' women's, labour, technological and economic history, and 'Parr gives the boot to neo-classical analysis, simplistic Marxism, and radical feminism' (p. 218). He quotes its introduction that 'the parts and proportions of the social landscape covered by class and gender alter' (p. 10) but finds that in the 1949 Paris strike 'she has suppressed the impact of class where it was undeniably a crucial force' (p. 220). From her own figures he suggests that 'the portrait of the "women's town" may be slightly misleading' (p. 219). He also finds that she downplays the wars and the state and 'seldom makes any reference to the considerable Canadian literature on work, class, gender, or small-town life' (pp. 220–21). He concludes that she 'has pushed us onto new terrain where gender is neither ignored nor is it given a monocausal explanatory force' (p. 221). Scheinberg (Archivaria, 1991) sees 'a more dynamic alternative to the old and stale studies that focused more on workers' industrial and organizational activities', while doubting conclusions drawn from 'the testimony of seven women' (p. 175). Dennis (EcHR, 1991) calls it 'an important contribution to the literature of labour history and locality studies' (p. 762). A contribution from inside the field's gender strand, alongside Sangster (1989) and Bradbury (1993). It does not claim that labour history lacked gender before 1990. edge_842 and edge_889 (cdn_women_gender → cdn_working_class) already carry the entry-level contribution and critique.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: gender_family_class ('Gender, family and class') holds Sangster, Parr and Bradbury and cites cdnsrc_parr_1990. The kind is contribution. Her 1985 criticism of how labour and women's historians treated skill is recorded here rather than as a separate critique edge: see edges_considered_not_proposed.

proposed_edges.relationship: British child immigrants as labouring children (1977–80), and childhood as a history of power (1985)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: In-period. Her Yale PhD (1977), 'The Home Children: British Juvenile Immigrants to Canada, 1868–1924', is recorded in the AHA Directory of History Dissertations (record 45612; adviser Robin Winks). Drystek's review of Labouring Children (Archivaria 11, 1980–81, read in full) names the thesis as the source of its sample of 997 Barnardo case histories (p. 241). He quotes the book's aims: a 'study of the life and work of child immigrants in Britain and Canada' (p. 13) that would 'reveal a darker side of evangelicalism, of turn-of-the-century childhood, and of Canadian rural life than the record has so far been allowed to express' (p. 12). His reading is critical: 'because of the authors' almost uniformly negative approach, the study is of limited value', the sample's statistical basis is unexplained, and 'the argument that a British child immigrant suffered a special burden is not convincing' (pp. 241–42). The book itself is unread here. Her own words (Atlantis, 1985) turn the subject into a question about power: she finds it troubling to treat women and children 'as part of one subject', admits to being 'part of a group who wrote, reviewed, lectured and squabbled this cluster into convention', and asks 'Is it nature which ties women and children together as subjects? Clearly not' (p. 39); the family 'is experienced by members of different generations in very different ways' (p. 44). She also edited Childhood and Family in Canadian History (1982; title-level, see edge_792). A contribution among the field's early works, not its origin: Sutherland's Children in English-Canadian Society (1976) precedes it.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: family_economy ('Family economies and child labour') holds Parr and Bradbury and cites Labouring Children and the 1982 collection.

proposed_edges.relationship: Disaggregating the sexual division of labour: gender and class compared across workplaces, read beyond Canada (1988–93)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: In-period, her own words: the CSSH article of 1988 (first-page extract read, p. 511) observes that 'economists and feminist theorists have been interested in sexual divisions as general features of the economic or sex/gender system rather than as boundaries between tasks forged in defined contexts by particular clashes of interest', and that 'most analysts have dealt with gender division as a characteristic of the work force as a whole'. Reviews of The Gender of Breadwinners outside Canada (all read in full): Benson (JAH, 1993, p. 1630) writes that 'few historians have successfully integrated the discussion of these two fundamental relationships' and that 'Parr joins this small but growing group'. On p. 1631 Benson continues: 'Like others influenced by post-structuralist theory, she emphasizes the shifting and multivalent meanings often obscured by dualisms'; Parr 'gives gender and class coordinate roles in her analysis but downplays ethnicity'. Dennis (EcHR, 1991) finds that she 'goes far beyond previous accounts of connections between capitalism and patriarchy' (p. 761) but faults graphs that 'cavalierly use straight lines to connect a handful of isolated observations' (p. 762). Bertaux (JEH, 1992) wants 'a basic quantitative summary of work force data' (p. 240) but concludes that 'the topic of gender and work is not strictly a "women's issue"' (p. 241). The book itself is unread here. This records reception in international journals, not adoption. Optional: edge_840 (cdn_women_gender → gender) already links the Canadian field to the international entry.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: class_family ('Gender, class and family': Clark; Davidoff and Hall; Taylor) is the closest strand. Her 1985 essay cites Barbara Taylor's Eve and the New Jerusalem (n. 2), a work in this strand. studer_class_reception concerns Studer and Frevert and does not fit.
proposed_edges.include_note: Kept at release (1.136): edge_840 links the Canadian field to the international gender entry; this edge records something different, the reception of Parr's own comparative method (gender and class compared across two towns) in international economic- and labour-history journals (Dennis, Bertaux, Benson), read in full.

proposed_edges.relationship: Postwar Canadian consumption as a politics of nation, class and gender: domestic goods, designers and householders (1999)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: In-period, her own words: the abstract of 'Household Choices as Politics and Pleasure in 1950s Canada' (ILWCH 55, 1999, a special issue on class and consumption) reads 'How much consumption matters is a cultural difference, a shared national predicament, a politics grounded in the circumstances of class, and learned as a gendered responsibility', and asks 'When producers were not paramount in the regulation of consumption, to what priorities was commerce subsidiary?' Domestic Goods (1999) is unread here; as Brush quotes it (EH.NET, 2000, read in full), it is 'an archeology of the material, moral, and economic choices and constraints which formed Canadian commodity culture in the two decades after the Second World War' (p. 17). It asks 'How much can citizens talk back to manufacturers and the state about domestic goods?' (pp. 3–4). It sets itself against accounts that 'naturalize[d] these hortatory American norms as the intrinsic qualities of "consumer society"' (p. 11), and it places studies of material culture 'into unaccustomed company' (p. 3). Brush notes that Parr 'locates the history of consumption as a history primarily of women as consumers, in contrast to the male-dominated fields of design and manufacturing'. Criticism: Owram (BC Studies 129, 2001, read in full) finds the book's 'strength is in its parts rather than in some seamless thesis' (p. 103). He reads her as arguing that 'the assumption of consumer sovereignty is facile' (p. 104), and answers that 'Canadians, both men and women, preferred Fords to Volvos, and that is what they got' (p. 105). edge_843 (cdn_women_gender ↔ consumption, comparison) is title-level; this edge adds read evidence.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: gender_consumption ('Investigate the division of family labor, male and female consumer identities, class differences and state definitions; avoid one universal consumer') fits the 1999 abstract's nation, class and gender. household_labor (de Vries) is the alternative.

proposed_edges.relationship: Embodied, sensory histories of megaprojects and environmental change in Canada, 1953–2003 (2006–10)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Dated 2006–2011; no claim here concerns her work before 2000. Sensing Changes: Technologies, Environments, and the Everyday, 1953–2003 (UBC Press, 2010) is unread here. As Jackson quotes it (Senses and Society 6:2, 2011, read in full), Parr seeks to move beyond 'representations . . . in language . . . , to open interpretive space in which to study the robust materiality of technologies, environments, and the everyday, to encounter them as directly and as fleshly as possible' (p. 9). Jackson describes chapters on the NATO base at Gagetown, nuclear power and heavy water on Lake Huron, the St Lawrence Seaway at Iroquois, the Columbia River reservoir and Walkerton's water, each read through a sense ('Smell and Risk', 'Taste and Expertise'). She adds that Parr counts proprioception, kinesthetics and proxemics among the senses (pp. 225–27). Jackson places the book in the UBC Press Nature/History/Culture series (p. 225). Rumiel (Left History 15:1, 2011, read in full) notes 'the people whose lives and senses of self had been transformed' by megaprojects (p. 189). She suggests that 'a comparative analysis of a related case in a Canadian Aboriginal or Inuit community' was a missed opportunity (p. 189). The environmental line begins earlier with 'Smells Like?: Sources of Uncertainty in the History of the Great Lakes Environment' (Environmental History 11:2, 2006; metadata only). A contribution: it records her later field, not influence on environmental history's formation.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: No environment strand covers Canadian, embodied or sensory environmental history; the nearest, environmental_justice_organizing and wilderness_culture, do not fit. A new strand (for example 'Bodies, senses and environmental change') could be added at release if more such entries follow.

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: Considered, not proposed as a separate edge. In 1985 she criticised, in her own words, the way 'students of men's work and men's participation in labour organisations' had 'reified the skill-unskill boundary' (p. 42). The same sentence names women's historians and historians of childhood. Her worked example of an inadequate Marxist analysis is Women at Work (1975), a women's-history collection, with Lowe's 1982 sociology. No labour-history work is named, so a critique aimed at cdn_working_class or at its class_culture_community strand would overstate her target. The criticism is quoted on rel_02, and edge_889 carries the feminist critique of labour history at entry level. If reviewers want a person-level critique, rel_02 could be re-typed as critique, citing p. 42.

Not proposed. Her 1985 criticism of the mid-1970s 'maternal feminism' framing (p. 41) comes from inside her own field and names no atlas entry's position beyond the earlier_witnesses_and_collections literature in general. It is quoted on rel_01; a critique edge parallel to a contribution edge on the same target would confuse the map.
Leads, not proposed: neither has a person entry, and the brief asks for edges from Parr. Heron (1991) and Sangster (1996) are the clearest in-period critics, and both are quoted on rel_01 and rel_02.

A strong lead, not proposed. Domestic Goods' third section is 'on household technology' (Brush quoting p. 10). Her site lists articles in Technology and Culture: 'What Makes Washday Less Blue?' (1997), the introduction to 'Modern Kitchen, Good Home, Strong Nation' (2003), and 'Classics Reconsidered: Ruth Schwartz Cowan's More Work for Mother' (2005). Queen's University's notice of her death (16 May 2024) records the Society for the History of Technology's Edelstein Prize for Sensing Changes and its Leonardo da Vinci Medal (2018). None of the Technology and Culture texts was read. The 2005 Cowan reconsideration could support an edge to the technology/households strand, possibly a critique, once read.

Not proposed. Dennis (EcHR, 1991) reads the book as labour history and locality studies, but the international reviews read here frame it mainly as gender-and-class history (rel_04). The Canadian working-class edge (rel_02) carries the labour-history claim.

Not proposed. Labouring Children and 'The Skilled Emigrant and her Kin' (CHR, 1987) are migration studies, but she has no roster row there and the 1987 article was not read. Benson (1993) and Scheinberg (1991) also note that ethnicity is secondary in the 1990 book.

Not proposed. Reviewers note her oral-history projects (Scheinberg 1991) and the Megaprojects New Media site (Rumiel 2011), and Canadian PhD co-citation points to oral and digital history. These are methods in her work, not claims about those fields that a read text supports.

Not proposed. The Canadian PhD co-citation field that reads her most is 'Moral regulation, gender, sexuality & the body'. That is reading data, not a claim, and nothing read here ties her work to the moral-regulation framework.

source_addenda.cdnsrc_sangster_1995: Addendum 2026-10-14 (Claude, Parr draft): read in full in an Internet Archive capture (4 September 2024) of the journal PDF (lh.journals.yorku.ca/index.php/lh/article/download/5312/4507); the live site is behind a bot check. Pages 109–21 by running head. On p. 120 she calls The Gender of Breadwinners 'One of the path breaking books on gender history', written 'by Joy Parr, an established historian', in arguing that there is no 'definite age split' between women's and gender historians. She cites Palmer's 'Canadian Controversies' (History Today, 1994) on gender history's 'parochialism' (p. 120 n. 34).
source_addenda.cdnsrc_dubinsky_marks_1996: Addendum 2026-10-14 (Claude, Parr draft): read in full in an Internet Archive capture (15 February 2020) of the journal PDF (article/download/6967/6151). Pages 205–20 by running head. They answer Sangster's dichotomies, citing Parr's Gender of Breadwinners (p. 209 n. 6). 'As Joy Parr has recently shown, an understanding of identity requires a willingness to refrain from imposing one category - be it class or gender - on historical actors' (p. 211, n. 11: the 1990 book and the 1995 CHR essay). They defend attention to age, marital status and religion as well as gender, race and class (pp. 210–11).
source_addenda.cdnsrc_iacovetta_kealey_1996: Addendum 2026-10-14 (Claude, Parr draft): read in full in an Internet Archive capture (9 February 2020) of the journal PDF (article/download/6968/6152). Pages 221–37 by running head. 'Joy Parr, recognized as a leading practitioner of gender history' (p. 222). 'a major figure in the field, Joy Parr, says that "gender history made masculinity and femininity commensurably problematical historically, while insisting that neither could be well understood without companion inquiries into the other hierarchies with which they were mutually intertwined"' (p. 228, n. 13: CHR 1995, pp. 362–63). Gender history's stress on discourse, 'discourses are the medium through which experiences are comprehensible' (p. 229, n. 15: Parr 1995, p. 365). 'one of the key problems with the gender history approach - how to understand the "whys" and the "whos" rather than the "hows"' (p. 229). They propose treating gender history 'as an approach/epistemology rather than as a field in direct competition with women's history' (p. 228).
source_addenda.cdnsrc_sangster_1996: Addendum 2026-10-14 (Claude, Parr draft): read in full in an Internet Archive capture (15 February 2020) of the journal PDF (article/download/6970/6154). Pages 239–48 by running head. In n. 2 (p. 240) she quotes Parr's 'Gender History and Historical Practice' (in Parr and Rosenfeld, eds., Gender and History in Canada, 1996, p. 11) and says it tends 'to locate critics of gender history, feminist and anti-feminist alike, in the same oppositional group'. In n. 3 (p. 240) she notes she was reproached for not offering 'more criticism of historians such as Mariana Valverde and Joy Parr'. On p. 244 she quotes Parr (p. 14) that the move to gender 'began from the post-structuralist premise that identities were made in relationships', adding that the two 'have blossomed in tandem'. She concedes she had 'congealed and possibly blurred two issues' (p. 244). She questions 'the prevailing assumption that gender history as the field, post-structuralism as the method, equals a superior, more broad-minded history' (p. 246; n. 14 cites Parr p. 21).
